# Preface: How to Use This Book {.unnumbered epub:type=preface}

```{python}
#| label: preface-setup
# The two projects' headline facts: London's most visited ALVA member attraction, and the
# years the water analysis covers (its own settings).
import pandas as pd

from scripts import water as w
from scripts.facts import checked, fact

A = w.A
att = pd.read_csv("../examples/london/data/attractions.csv")
visits_col = next(c for c in att.columns if c.startswith("visits_"))

```

Change one number in a dataset, and how many documents are now wrong? If the number was
copied by hand into a report, a slide, an email and a web page, nobody knows without
searching. This book teaches a way of publishing with nothing to search for: you write once,
in plain text, and a web page, a Word document, a PDF, slides, an e-book, a website, a blog
and a dashboard all rebuild from that one source with one command. The program that rebuilds
them is Quarto.

This book is about producing publication-quality documents that are reproducible from their
data and code, at a speed that coding agents have only recently made possible. *Reproducible*
means every number, table and figure is computed by code from the data, kept beside the prose,
so one command rebuilds them all and anyone can check how they were made. *Publication
quality* means each output is fit for the reader who will use it: laid out, captioned, cited
and checked. The *speed* comes from the agent. The cryptic commands and fragile configuration
that used to stand between an analysis and its published, interactive form are no longer the
bottleneck: you describe the step, the agent writes the code and runs the commands, and you
check the result.

Quarto is one of three parts. With *git*, which records every version of the source, and a
hosting service such as GitHub Pages, which puts the result on the web, it lets one person
produce reproducible, publication-quality work for a wide range of settings and formats: a page
read on a phone, a report printed for a meeting, slides on a projector, an e-book, an interactive
dashboard. A coding agent does the typing for all three, and this book shows you how to
direct it and check its work.

## Prompt, Check, Publish {.unnumbered #prompt-check-publish}

The title names the method, a loop you run at every step of every project. You **prompt** a
*coding agent*, a program that writes files and runs commands at your request, describing
one small piece of work with its files and columns named. It is an *agent*, not a chat,
because it acts: where a web chat replies with code for you to copy and run, an agent edits
your files and runs the commands itself, then reports back. You **check** what it did: read
what changed, look at the result, compare it with the data. An agent can be fluent, fast
and wrong, so this step is never skipped, and it is always yours. Then Quarto **publishes**,
rebuilding every output from the checked source the same way every time. Chapter 1 explains
why the last step can be trusted, and Chapter 2 how to make the first two reliable.

Every hands-on step from Part II on goes once round the loop in @fig-loop.

![Prompt, Check, Publish: the loop this book teaches, with who acts at each step.](media/diagrams/loop){#fig-loop .on-light fig-alt="The loop. Prompt: you ask a coding agent for one small step, naming the files and ending with a check; Chapter 2. The agent does the work: it writes files and runs commands. Check: you read what changed, open the result and compare it with the data; Chapter 2. If it is not right, you fix the prompt and go round again. The checked source goes to Publish: Quarto's quarto render rebuilds every output, the same way every time; Chapter 1. Then the next step begins with a new prompt. Small steps, each one checked, every output rebuilt from one source."}

## Who this book is for {.unnumbered}

I wrote this book for analysts, researchers, data scientists, machine-learning engineers,
technical founders, educators and students: anyone who works with data and code and needs to
share the results. Most of all it is for people who publish numbers that change: the analyst
whose monthly pack is copied into Word and PowerPoint by hand, the researcher whose figures must
survive a resubmission, the engineer who writes up every evaluation three times, for a report,
a deck and a page, and the founder who sends investors a figure from the wrong month. It shows
how to publish everything from one plain-text source, prose and code together, with Quarto.
Quarto is free and open source, and it is traditional software, not AI, so the same source
always builds the same report, slide deck or web page: reproducible, interactive and of
publication quality. With a coding agent, work that once took days now takes minutes. Along
the way, I explain the concepts, the arguments and the decisions behind each step.

Reproducibility is why I wrote this book. Work that others can rebuild earns their trust,
justifies the decisions made on it, and gives them something to build on, which is how science,
technology and understanding move forward. More automation means fewer errors and a better
experience, for the people who make the work and for those who read it.

Publishing is half the job; the other half is being read. Content works only if it engages the
people it is for, so the book treats every output as something a particular reader will use,
and checks it as that reader would. I hope it improves the interactions, and the outcomes, of
everyone who works with data, software and AI applications and has to communicate them.

**Start-ups** get a particular kind of value from it, and should know its limits. The method
pays where a young company's numbers change: the monthly investor update, the benchmark or
evaluation white paper, the per-customer report, the documentation site. A small team that
already lives in a repository with an agent gets it almost for free, and the checking habit
keeps a wrong number away from an investor. It pays less where design or co-editing dominates:
the designed pitch deck, the marketing site and the plan the co-founders comment on in a shared
document can stay where they are (@sec-wrong-tool).

You may be new to Quarto, to coding agents or to both. No programming is assumed: I explain
the Python the agent writes, but you do not have to write it. If the terminal is new to you,
@sec-setup teaches the little you need, one checked step at a time, and @sec-first-report has
you use it by hand on a real report before you give an agent its first edit. @sec-terminal
collects the keys, paths and error messages worth knowing. The book's code is Python; Quarto
runs R just as well, through knitr, but this book does not teach it.

You will need a computer on which you can install software (Windows, Mac or Linux), a free
GitHub account, and an account with one coding agent (@sec-before-setup lists what each
needs). If you cannot install software, a ready-made environment in your browser will do
(@sec-codespace), and @sec-before-setup gives a low-cost route to an agent.

## Free and open source, nearly all the way {.unnumbered #open-source}

Almost everything this book uses is free and open-source software: you may use it, read its
source, change it and share it, at no cost, on any computer you like. Ubuntu, the Linux that
Windows readers install and many servers run; the terminal and its shell; Git; Python and the
packages the projects use, pandas, matplotlib and scikit-learn; uv; Jupyter's kernel; and the
publishing chain itself, [Quarto](https://quarto.org/license.html) (MIT License),
[Pandoc](https://github.com/jgm/pandoc/blob/main/COPYRIGHT) (GNU GPL) and
[Typst](https://github.com/typst/typst/blob/main/LICENSE) (Apache License 2.0).
The sites are plain static files that any web server can host.

That matters for more than price. A report built from open tools can be rebuilt by anyone,
anywhere, years from now, without a licence, an account or the permission of the company that
made the tools: the reproducibility this book is about depends on it. Open formats and open
tools also mean no lock-in: the source of every document is plain text you own, and moving it
to another tool, or another host, is a copy.

The exception is the coding agent. The program on your computer may itself be open source
([OpenAI's Codex CLI](https://github.com/openai/codex) is published under the Apache License
2.0, as [Google's Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli) was;
[Anthropic's Claude Code](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code) is not), but the models that do the reasoning are proprietary and run
on the vendors' servers, and using them usually costs money; @sec-before-setup gives the free
tier and the low-cost routes. That is the state of things as this book is written (licences
checked 2026-11-18), not a law of nature. Open models, and free agents that run them, may
change it, and nothing else in the method would need to change: the agent is the one part you
could swap without touching a single source file.

## The three running examples {.unnumbered}

Every concept is tied to one of three projects, each built on real, cited data.

**A London visitor guide** (Part II). For the city's tourism office, you write one guide that
becomes a web page, a Word brief for partners, a printed flyer, a dashboard for managers and
a published website. Every visitor number in it, from the `{python} top_visits` visits to the
`{python} top_name` in `{python} visits_year` down, is computed from the counts published by
the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions.

**A model evaluation at a start-up** (the fast path and Part III). Acme Signals, a fictional
two-person company, ranks a bank's marketing contacts for its call centre and evaluates each
release of its model on the real UCI Bank Marketing data. You add Quarto to its existing
repository and publish one set of results as an evaluation report and a model card, every
number read from the results its own script computes.

**Drinking-water risk in Colombian municipalities** (the water analysis, Part IV). You group Colombia's
municipal zones into kinds by water safety, services and context, from `{python} A.FIRST_YEAR`
to `{python} A.LAST_YEAR`, compare health and education outcomes between the kinds, and
publish the analysis as a report, slides, a blog post and a website, all from one analysis
script. Most of the data are Colombian open data, joined by official municipality codes;
rainfall comes from the Climate Hazards Center's CHIRPS data and altitude from NASA's SRTM
elevation data (@sec-sources).

## How the book is organised {.unnumbered}

**Part I** covers what you need first: what Quarto does (@sec-quarto) and how to work with a
coding agent safely (@sec-assistant), then one of two routes. The fast path (@sec-fast-path)
adds Quarto to an existing repository; the route from zero sets up your computer
(@sec-setup) and has you make a first report by hand (@sec-first-report): render it, check it
against its data, record it with Git and undo a change yourself before an agent makes one. The
GitHub account it asks for is free; an agent's account may not be.
`{python} fact("agents.claude_code_cost")` (checked `{python} checked("agents.claude_code_cost")`;
@sec-before-setup lists what each agent needs, and a low-cost route). **Part II** builds the
London guide, one format at a time, and is the foundations in depth. **Part III** is the craft
of the outputs professionals are asked for, from one set of evaluation results.
**Part IV**, the water analysis, builds a full analysis with the statistics explained on the
way. Each project ends by changing an input or a setting and explaining what the rebuild
changed. The **afterword** offers three projects that carry the method into your own work, a
metrics brief, a research supplement and a coursework report, each rebuilt from a fresh copy
of its repository ([Afterword](afterword.qmd#sec-afterword)). The appendices hold the Windows
setup, the terminal's keys and habits, a cheatsheet, troubleshooting, every checkpoint, the
data sources, how this book is built, and the facts that change, with their dates.

By the end of the book you will be able to:

- explain how Quarto turns one source into many formats, and why every rebuild gives the same
  result;
- direct a coding agent safely: a folder of its own, written rules, one step per prompt, each
  ending in a check, and larger tasks only when their checks can run without you;
- add Quarto to an existing repository, and review an agent's change as a pull request and a
  fresh clone;
- publish one set of results to several readers, guarding every sentence whose words depend
  on the data;
- predict which outputs a changed input will update, and check that the rebuild did exactly
  that.

## Your first afternoon {.unnumbered #first-afternoon}

Part I fits in an afternoon, and it ends with something to show for it. @sec-quarto and
@sec-assistant are reading: nothing to install, nothing to type. If you already use a terminal
and Git, @sec-fast-path takes you from there to a report in three formats in under an hour.
Otherwise, @sec-setup sets up your computer in six steps, each with a check; allow about an
hour. @sec-first-report is the first payoff, about 45 minutes at
the keyboard: you copy a small report, render it yourself, check its numbers against the data
and find the one that is wrong, start a Git history, change an input and undo it, and make
three common mistakes on purpose to read their errors. Everything in it is typed by hand
except the last step, the agent's first edit, which you check with Git before you keep it.

## What a hands-on step looks like {.unnumbered #how-the-hands-on-parts-work}

Each step is a three-part box, explained in @sec-boxes: the exact prompt to give your
agent, what it will probably run, and the few things only you can do. Prompts are
examples, not transcripts: agents vary, so check the result rather than the wording. Five
kinds of aside step out of the main text; here is one of each.

::: why
A number computed from the data cannot disagree with the data. Asides like this one explain
the mechanism behind a step, so that you can adapt it to your own project.
:::

::: pitfall
A render started while a live preview is rendering the same file collides with it. Asides
like this one describe failures seen in practice, and how to avoid them.
:::

::: practice
Ask for one step per prompt: a small change is quick to check, and when something breaks you
know which step broke it. Asides like this one hold judgement calls and habits.
:::

::: think
The agent reports a render with no errors. Is the work checked?

Not yet: a clean render proves that the code ran, not that its numbers are right. Asides like
this one ask a question to answer before you read on; the answer follows it.
:::

::: tryit
Asides like this one are exercises. Think of one document you produce more than once, and
note where each of its numbers comes from.

::: done
you can say which of its numbers are typed by hand and which come from a file.
:::
:::

Steps marked *optional* are for readers who are ahead; nothing later depends on them.

## Three ways through {.unnumbered}

**By role.** Follow your path in @tbl-reading-paths. Each hands-on chapter ends at a
checkpoint or at a finished example, where you can stop and resume later.

**The core path.** Parts II and IV are long because they explain, but the path through them
is shorter. On a first reading, leave for later the sections marked *(optional)* in their
headings, the water analysis's further challenges and its route that builds the model rather than using
it: nothing later depends on them. What remains is the core:

- **Part II:** Markdown and the guide's rules (@sec-markdown); computed numbers and one source
  in three formats (@sec-compute); three audiences from one prompt (@sec-audiences); Git,
  publishing and one changed input (@sec-publish).
- **Part III:** one set of results, a model card and a report (@sec-results), after the fast
  path (@sec-fast-path).
- **The water analysis:** the question, the data and the rules (@sec-water-question); one chapter for
  each step of the analysis, from exploring (@sec-explore) to the within-cluster check
  (@sec-causation), copying each block's finished script from clustering on (@sec-routes);
  then the report, the slides, the website and one changed setting (@sec-publish-many).

**Workshop-paced.** The book grew out of a six-hour workshop and keeps its shape, while
explaining what the workshop only had time to show: why each step works, where it fails, and
when not to take it. @sec-workshop has the day's agenda and the chapters each block covers
(@tbl-agenda and @tbl-agenda-water).

## When you get stuck {.unnumbered #when-you-fall-behind}

You will get stuck: an install fails, a prompt goes wrong, a render stops with an error you
have never seen. That is expected, and the book is built for it. Every hands-on block ends at
a *checkpoint*, a folder in the workshop's repository (`checkpoints/`), the copy of the
workshop's files you download during setup (@sec-step-check). It holds the project as it
should be at that point, with a README listing the steps to catch up. In a workshop the rule
is simple: **stuck for two minutes, catch up**. Where the book reaches a checkpoint, a catch-up
box gives the one line to paste into your agent (@fig-catch-up).

Reading on your own, you have time the room does not, so spend a few minutes on a diagnosis
first. Each step uses only what @sec-setup and @sec-first-report teach:

1. **Where are you?** `pwd` prints the folder; the project's commands work only inside it.
2. **What changed?** `git status` lists the files changed since your last commit, and
   `git diff` shows how, including changes you did not mean to make.
3. **What does the error say?** Read its first line
   ([Reading an error](appendices/b-terminal.qmd#sec-keys-errors)) and look it up in @sec-troubleshooting.
4. **Try one fix**, the one that line points to, and run the command again.

If that fix does not work, catch up. Afterwards, make one short check of your own: open the
output that the checkpoint's README names, and see that it shows what the book describes at
that point.

![Catching up from a checkpoint. Your work is backed up first, so nothing is lost.](media/diagrams/catch-up){#fig-catch-up .on-light fig-alt="Stuck for two minutes, you paste the line Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/NN/README.md into the agent. It follows four steps. One, back up your project folder, all but its .venv environment, to a new time-stamped folder beside it. Two, copy the checkpoint in, and for the water project the data if they are missing. Three, render and check a named output. Four, carry on reading from the catch-up box: the project now matches the book at that point."}

The README's last step names the workshop slide to rejoin at. In the book, that place is the
catch-up box itself, so after catching up you carry on reading from the box. If you were stuck
partway through a block, go straight to its box: the checkpoint already holds the steps between
where you stopped and the box. @sec-checkpoints lists every checkpoint.

## Two editions {.unnumbered #two-editions}

This book comes as an e-book (EPUB) and as a website, built from the same source: it is its
own first example of the method. The [website edition](https://project-delphi.github.io/quarto-workshop/book/)
runs everything interactive: the 3-D scenes of the London map, the k-means steps, the
clusters and Colombia's relief, and two data explorers. The e-book shows each as an animation
or a still, with a link to the live version (the first, the London map, also has a QR code).
Readers that cannot play animations show the first frame, designed as a useful still, and the
website respects your reduced-motion setting.

## Versions and dates {.unnumbered}

The book was built and checked with Quarto 1.10.20 (with its bundled Typst 0.15), Python 3.12
and uv, in November 2026. Facts that change, such as a model's price, an agent's account
or a free hosting plan's limits, carry the date they were checked, and are kept in one place,
@sec-facts, which a rebuild updates everywhere they appear. Some will have changed by the
time you read them; the principles around them
should not have.

Chapter 1 needs nothing installed: start there.
